rv.q: Hairspray may be a bubblegum-pink sherbet-dip of a show, but it's also an incandescent doo-wop hymn to the emerging teen culture of the 1960s.
Jack O'Brien's production has jet fuel running through its veins, thanks to Jerry Mitchell's formation choreography, William Ivey Long's colourful costumes and David Rockwell's cartoon sets.
Its arrival is worth the wait, and its two hours of musical theatre joy heralds the return of large-scale musicals to the West End following a barren spell.
This show really does pronounce theatre open again.
Lizzie Bea is terrific as Tracy, but she has a job keeping the limelight from Michael Ball.
Ultimately, you'd have to be a pretty miserable soul not to enjoy this uplifting belter of a musical.
Indeed if the West End still has a heart beat you can hear it loud and clear with the return of Hairspray .
Ultimately, Hairspray is a great big hug of a show.
Hairspray has perfected the recipe of a crowd-pleasing cocktail.

cn.t: Critics enthusiastically celebrate Hairspray's return as a joyful, big-hearted musical spectacle. The show earns praise for its infectious energy, irresistible score, and uplifting message, with standout performances delivering exactly the euphoric fix audiences need.

vr.q: I give Hairspray what else five stars
